title: City growth can coexist with concentrated opportunity gaps, making inclusion a productivity, mobility, and legitimacy problem
source_unit: OECD, What Works for Inclusive Growth in Cities, OECD Urban Studies, 2026
geography: More than 600 European Union cities, OECD/EC city policy survey, and selected city interventions including Barcelona, Tromsø, Lisbon, Madrid, Milan, Düsseldorf, Cluj-Napoca, and Stockholm

observations.period: 2026 report; more than 600 EU cities and inclusive-growth outcomes

denominator.unit: European Union cities analysed by the OECD, approximately more than

growth_inclusion_gap.value: higher productivity and GDP growth are not always associated with lower poverty, reduced inequality, or improved access to opportunity; poverty reduction has stalled or reversed in many large cities

urban_poverty_social_exclusion.unit: urban residents at risk of poverty or social exclusion across the European Union

childhood_disadvantage_cost.unit: percent of GDP annually; estimated cost across EU OECD countries through lost employment, earnings, and health outcomes

inequality_growth_association.unit: percentage-point reduction in annual GDP-per-capita growth associated with a 3-point increase in the Gini coefficient

observations.method: OECD comparative analysis of city-level economic, poverty, inequality, opportunity, and spatial indicators, supplemented by policy and intervention evidence.
observations.uncertainty: The report combines descriptive cross-city associations, estimates, and selected intervention evidence; these measures do not establish that city growth or inequality alone caused the reported outcomes.
observations.subgroup: Urban residents facing barriers in education, employment, housing, mobility, health, public services, and climate protection, with attention to young people, low-income households, and people with migrant backgrounds.
observations.counterinterpretation: High productivity can create fiscal and employment capacity for later redistribution or service improvement; a growth-inclusion gap does not mean growth is harmful or that every city follows the same trajectory.

observations.period: 2026 report; intra-urban access to mobility and green space

denominator.unit: urban residents in large and mid-sized EU cities

transit_access_gap.unit: approximately one in three residents unable to reach public transport within a ten-minute walk

green_space_gap.unit: approximately one in four residents lacking access to green space

life_chance_route.value: transport and green-space gaps limit access to jobs, services, and quality of life and disproportionately affect young people, low-income households, and people with migrant backgrounds

spatial_concentration.value: income, employment, health, and service disadvantages often overlap within the same neighbourhoods

observations.method: OECD city-level analysis of access, neighbourhood conditions, and multidimensional inequality within and across cities.
observations.uncertainty: The summary reports approximate access shares and does not measure trip reliability, affordability, safety, actual use, or household-level mobility outcomes for every city.
observations.subgroup: Young people, low-income households, residents of underserved neighbourhoods, people with migrant backgrounds, and people dependent on public transport or public green space.
observations.counterinterpretation: Car access, cycling, local services, remote work, and other forms of mobility or amenity can partly offset measured ten-minute access gaps; proximity is not the same as usable access.

refugee_language_employment.unit: percent of refugees entering employment within six months in the Tromsø language-introduction example

housing_first_sustainment.unit: percent housing sustainment in the Lisbon Housing First example

youth_transport_employment.unit: percentage-point increase in probability of finding employment after job loss associated with the Madrid youth transport pass example

desegregation.value: Barcelona school desegregation narrowed the educational achievement gap by nearly three points for disadvantaged students in standardised tests

observations.method: OECD synthesis of selected city practices and reported evaluations or impact evidence across education, language, housing, and mobility interventions.
observations.uncertainty: These are selected examples with different designs, populations, outcomes, and comparison strategies; they should not be treated as a common effect size or universal city-policy estimate.
observations.subgroup: Disadvantaged students, refugees, people experiencing homelessness or substance-use challenges, and workers who lost employment and need mobility access.
observations.counterinterpretation: Program effects may depend on local institutional capacity, selection, complementary services, and funding; replication without those conditions may not produce the same results.

denominator.unit: cities responding to the OECD/EC survey

inclusive_education_priority.unit: percent of surveyed cities prioritising inclusive education

inequality_inclusion_priority.unit: percent of surveyed cities prioritising reducing inequality and fostering inclusion

departmental_silos.unit: percent or approximately of cities still implementing inclusive growth through departmental silos

enablers.value: the report identifies long-term cross-government strategy, participatory design, granular neighbourhood data, sustainable finance, dedicated teams, monitoring and adaptation, and sustained communication as enabling factors

observations.method: OECD/European Commission city-policy survey and synthesis of implementation, participation, financing, data, delivery-capacity, monitoring, and political-support conditions.
observations.uncertainty: Reported priorities and organisational arrangements do not prove implementation quality, resident influence, funding adequacy, or improved outcomes; survey coverage and self-reporting may limit comparability.
observations.subgroup: City administrations, neighbourhood residents, community organisations, service users, local employers, and groups affected by cross-departmental policy gaps.
observations.counterinterpretation: Departmental structures can provide accountability and expertise; integration may create coordination costs or dilute responsibility if roles and resources are unclear.

related_sources.claim: Official OECD DOI and publication record for the 163-page report.
OECD local-data context for city and neighbourhood measurement.

boundary: This record adds a comparative within-city opportunity and implementation layer to the urban-capacity route. It combines OECD city analysis, survey evidence, and selected intervention examples; it is not respondent-level longitudinal data, not a universal causal estimate, and not evidence that all listed policies have the same effect outside their local settings.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: The official OECD executive-summary page was reviewed for the 600-plus-city comparison, poverty and inequality findings, mobility and green-space access, five policy pillars, selected intervention examples, city survey priorities, departmental silos, and enabling factors.
